claims.text: Large language models presented with clinical vignettes containing planted errors hallucinate by elaborating on false details in 50% to 82% of cases across models and prompting methods.
Prompt-based mitigation reduces the mean hallucination rate across tested large language models from 66% to 44% (p < 0.001).
Prompt-based mitigation reduces the hallucination rate of GPT-4o from 53% to 23% (p < 0.001).
Temperature adjustments to 0 offer no significant improvement in reducing adversarial hallucination rates in large language models.
Short clinical vignettes show slightly higher odds of adversarial hallucination compared to long vignettes containing identical medical content.
Prompt engineering strategies reduce the frequency of adversarial hallucination errors but do not eliminate them.

evidence.description: Hallucination rates range from 50 % to 82 % across models and prompting methods in tests on 300 simulated clinical vignettes.
Prompt-based mitigation lowers the overall hallucination rate (mean across all models) from 66 % to 44 % (p < 0.001).
For the best-performing model, GPT-4o, rates decline from 53 % to 23 % (p < 0.001).
Temperature adjustments offer no significant improvement when testing six LLMs across 5,400 outputs.
Short vignettes show slightly higher odds of hallucination compared to long versions differing only in word count.
While prompt engineering reduces errors, it does not eliminate them, leaving residual error risk remaining in up to 23% or more of cases.

methodologies.name: Adversarial hallucination benchmark evaluation
methodologies.description: Evaluated six large language models using 300 physician-validated clinical vignettes with planted false details across standard, prompt mitigation, and deterministic temperature settings, generating 5,400 total outputs.

limitations.text: Prompt-based mitigation and deterministic temperature settings reduce hallucination rates but fail to eliminate adversarial hallucination risks entirely in clinical decision support contexts.
